shines with piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if seen by eyes through true reason; and by the confidence of his belief, he stands out among men as much as the sun outshines the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power, but by its divinity and holiness. Believe that this sun, O Asclepius, is second only to God, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly creatures, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living animal <note>the concept of the 'Anima Mundi' or World Soul, viewing the universe as a singular living organism</note> that always lives, and was, and is, and shall be, then nothing in the world is mortal. For in every single part of a living thing, which exists in the world just as in one and the same ever-living animal, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God must be most full of life and eternity himself, if it is necessary for him to live forever. Therefore, just as the world is eternal, so also the sun itself is forever the governor of living things, or the attendant and dispenser of their entire vitality. God, then, is the eternal governor of all living things or vital beings that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. Moreover, he has dispensed life once by an eternal law, providing life to all living things in this manner which I shall describe.

<summary>Hermes explains the sun's role as a divine governor and dispenser of life, second only to God, within a universe that is itself a single, eternal living organism.</summary>
<keywords>sun, Asclepius, World Soul, immortality, divine governance, eternity, vital spirit, cosmology</keywords>
